title: Lech Lecha: between the pieces (Genesis 15)
hookLine: a vision in deep darkness, a smoking furnace, and a promise of exile and return

lines: A TREE YOU'LL NEVER SIT UNDER.
cards: Some promises are quick: I'll call you back in five minutes. Some take years. A parent who plants a tree knowing they'll never sit in its shade.

Someone saving for a grandchild who isn't born yet. There's a strange feeling in those promises: you believe them, and you know you won't see them come true. Abram has been promised a land and a great nation.
Years have passed. He's still childless. One night God speaks to him again, and the promise gets much longer, and much darker, before it gets bright.
It's called the covenant between the pieces.

teach.b: It begins with God saying: fear not, Abram, I am thy shield. And Abram answers honestly: what good is any of it? I have no child.
So God brings him outside, under the night sky: "Look now toward heaven, and count the stars, if thou be able to count them." So shall your descendants be.
The Torah says Abram believed, and God counted it to him as righteousness. Then comes something ancient and strange. God tells Abram to bring a heifer, a goat, a ram, a turtledove and a young pigeon.
Abram cuts the animals in half and lays the halves opposite each other, with a path between. Birds of prey swoop down on the carcasses, and Abram drives them away.
In the ancient Near East, this is how you sealed a covenant: the parties walked between the pieces, as if to say, may this happen to me if I break my word. The sun goes down.

teach.h: A GREAT DARK DREAD: EXILE, THEN RETURN.
teach.b: A deep sleep falls on Abram, and a great dark dread. In the darkness, God tells him the hard part. Your descendants will be strangers in a land not theirs, enslaved and afflicted four hundred years.
Then that nation will be judged, and they'll come out with great wealth, and return here.

teach.h: A FURNACE AND A TORCH PASS THROUGH.
teach.b: Then, in the dark, a smoking furnace and a flaming torch pass between the pieces. Only God passes through. Abram doesn't.
The promise is one-sided. At the Passover seder, Jews still read about this night: God kept the promise made to Abraham between the pieces.
The promise was long. It went through darkness. And it came true.

how: Jews call Genesis 15 the brit bein habetarim, the covenant between the pieces, and recall it at the Passover seder in the Haggadah's passage on God keeping the promise to Abraham.

games.q: you're Abram, promised a great nation, but still childless after years. God says, fear not, I am thy shield. what do you say?
o: what good is it? I have no child.
games.why: Abram answers honestly, and God takes him outside to count the stars. then Abram believes.

practice: Think of something you hope for that won't happen soon, maybe not in your lifetime: healing in your family, peace somewhere, a change in the world.
Don't push it closer; let it stay far away, like stars, and feel the dark between now and then without rushing through it. Notice that you can hope for something you may not see.

wordCard.voice: Lech Lecha. The portion where Abram counts the stars, and a torch passes between the pieces, sealing a promise that runs through darkness.
